documents.title: EACVI recommendations on the use of echocardiography in adult cardiac surgery

chunks.content: 1 Introduction Atrial septal defects (ASDs) are the most common congenital heart defect that can be diagnosed in adulthood [ ]. ASD can be associated with atrial fibrillation, paradoxical embolism, right heart failure, and, in rare cases, pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). Device closure is the treatment of choice for most patients with a secundum ASD, which is the most common type of all ASDs [ ]. In patients with severe PAH with pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) of ≧5 Wood units (WU), fenestrated ASD closure may be considered when PVR falls below 5 WU after targeted PAH treatment and significant L‐R shunt is present [ ]. PAH therapy and subsequent defect closure as a treat‐and‐repair strategy is an effective approach in selected ASD patients [ ]. This report presents a case in which an L‐R shunt due to an ASD became apparent after PAH treatment. We suppose that decreased right ventricular (RV) compliance due to PAH contributes to the reduction of the L‐R shunt. 2 Case History/Examination The patient was a 51‐year‐old woman with no significant medical history. The patient had been experiencing worsening shortness of breath on exertion for the past year and was referred from a local dental clinic for a tooth extraction under sedation. Preoperative 12‐lead electrocardiogram showed ventricular premature contractions, and the patient was referred to our department. A subsequent echocardiogram raised suspicion of pulmonary hypertension (PH), leading to admission for further evaluation. On physical examination, an accentuated second heart sound (P2) was noted, and the fixed split was unclear. No hepatosplenomegaly or lower extremity edema was observed. The patient showed no clubbing of fingers, fingertip ulcers, or signs of Raynaud's phenomenon. The New York Heart Association functional classification was Grade II. Chest radiography revealed enlargement of the bilateral pulmonary arteries (Figure ). Electrocardiography revealed ventricular premature contractions, negative T waves in leads V 1 – V 4 , and deep S waves in leads V 5 – V 6 , indicating right ventricular overload (Figure ). No elevation in D‐dimer or brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) levels was found, and antinuclear antibody and collagen disease‐specific antibodies were negative. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed moderate tricuspid regurgitation, an elevated tricuspid regurgitant pressure gradient (TRPG) of 68 mmHg, with both systolic and diastolic flattening of the interventricular septum and enlargement of the right‐sided heart (Figure ). Left ventricular (LV) ejection fraction was preserved. We were unable to diagnose the ASD defects and shunt flow at the time of admission. The ventilation‐perfusion scan and contrast‐enhanced computed tomographic pulmonary angiography excluded the possibility of chronic thromboembolic pulmonary disease. The fraction of the right‐to‐left shunt was 6.6%, which was within the normal range. Pulmonary function test showed vital capacity (%VC) of 91.2%, one‐second forced expiratory volume (FEV 1.0 ) of 74.4%, and diffusing capacity (%DL CO ) of 79.3%. Hemodynamic evaluation with right heart catheterization (RHC) showed severe pre‐capillary PH (the mean pulmonary artery pressure [PAP] of 44 mmHg, and the PVR of 7.4 WU), and increased pulmonary‐to‐systemic flow ratio ( Q p / Q s ), suggesting the presence of an L–R shunt (Table ). 3 Differential Diagnosis In this case, the initial presentation with PAH without an obvious intracardiac shunt required careful consideration of differential diagnoses. The main differentials included idiopathic PAH, PAH associated with connective tissue disease, chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH), and congenital heart disease‐related PAH. Laboratory testing and autoimmune screening were negative, and ventilation‐perfusion scintigraphy excluded CTEPH. At this stage, a definitive diagnosis of ASD had not been established, as the oximetry run data showed variability and transthoracic echocardiography did not reveal any shunt flow. After medical therapy reduced PVR, a left‐to‐right shunt through a secundum ASD became evident, confirming the underlying congenital etiology of PAH. This case highlights that ASD‐related PAH can be clinically indistinguishable from idiopathic PAH when shunt flow is masked by elevated right‐sided pressures. 4 Conclusion and Results (Outcome and Follow‐Up) Three months after initiating combination therapy with Macitentan (10 mg/day) and Tadalafil (40 mg/day), transthoracic echocardiography visualized an abundant L‐R shunt across a secundum ASD (Figure ). Additionally, the TRPG decreased to 41 mmHg, and RV systolic function improved. As a result of the hemodynamic re‐evaluation 5 months after treatment, the mean PAP decreased to 26 mmHg, and PVR declined to 2.6 WU. The Q p / Q s increased from 1.6 to 2.2, shown in Table . Based on these findings, the patient was diagnosed with PAH associated with an ASD. Transesophageal echocardiography revealed a secundum ASD with a maximum diameter of 17 mm and a small ventricular septal defect (VSD) (Figure ). Both hemodynamically and anatomically, the ASD was determined to be correctable. The patient eventually underwent transcutaneous ASD closure using a 19.5‐mm Figulla Flex II at another hospital. Transesophageal echocardiography revealed a secundum ASD with a maximum diameter of 17 mm and a small ventricular septal defect (VSD) (Figure ). Both hemodynamically and anatomically, the ASD was determined to be correctable. The patient eventually underwent transcutaneous ASD closure using a 19.5‐mm Figulla Flex II at another hospital. After the closure, the TRPG decreased further to 32 mmHg along with a reduction in RV size on echocardiography. The patient is currently receiving combination therapy with two pulmonary vasodilators. Five months after ASD closure, the mean PAP was 14 mmHg, and the PVR was 1.8 WU (Table ). The Q p / Q s decreased to 0.92, suggesting a favorable treatment course and the presence of an insignificant VSD. We herein report a case in which the improvement in PVR and subsequent improved RV compliance due to pulmonary vasodilators revealed an ASD. It is crucial to suspect shunt disease as a potential cause of PH, and transesophageal echocardiography or agitated saline contrast studies should be considered to detect latent defects. 5 Discussion We present a case in which a diagnosis of ASD was established after the appearance of an L‐R shunt following targeted PAH treatment. Percutaneous defect closure was successfully performed as a treatment‐and‐repair strategy, and the patient had a favorable outcome. In this case, the improvement in RV compliance following PAH treatment is believed to have led to an increase in the L‐R shunt. Prior to treatment, the L‐R shunt was attenuated, which made the diagnosis difficult. The presence of intracardiac defects should be considered in all patients with PAH. To our knowledge, there have been no previous reports discussing this phenomenon and its underlying mechanism, and we present it here. 5.1 Diagnosis of <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">ASD</styled-content> by Echocardiography Due to a lack of early symptoms and the subtlety of physical findings, ASD can be undiagnosed until adulthood unless suspected and observed carefully. Echocardiography is the first‐line diagnostic examination, and RV volume overload is a clue suspecting the presence of ASD. Optimal echocardiographic imaging of the ASDs requires imaging from multiple windows, planes, and sweeps as well as the use of color flow Doppler [ ]. Apical four‐chamber views are notorious for giving false echo dropouts and false positive impressions of a defect [ ]. In addition to the standard views, the subcostal view, tilted parasternal view, and right chest wall approach are useful for detecting defects. The agitated saline contrast bubble study is also a non‐invasive and effective tool for screening systemic‐to‐pulmonary shunts. It is expected that essentially 100% of ASDs will be detected with a high‐quality agitated saline contrast bubble study that includes maneuvers (Valsalva, cough) to promote transient right‐to‐left shunting [ ]. For unusually located atrial defects such as sinus venosus type, transesophageal echocardiography, computed tomography, and cardiovascular magnetic resonance can be helpful for detecting anomalies and planning surgical repair. 5.2 Contributing Factors of the Interatrial Shunt in <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">ASD</styled-content> The shunt volume depends on RV/LV compliance, defect size, and left atrial (LA)/right atrial (RA) pressure. A simple ASD results in L‐R shunt because of the higher compliance of the RV compared with the LV, and causes RV volume overload and pulmonary overcirculation. Reduction in LV compliance, or any condition with elevation of LA pressure (hypertension, or various left heart diseases), increases L‐R shunt. On the other hand, reduced RV compliance (pulmonic stenosis, PAH, other RV disease) or tricuspid valve disease may decrease L‐R shunt or eventually cause shunt reversal, resulting in cyanosis [ ]. In this case, it is considered that the decrease in RV compliance associated with PH may have decreased the L‐R shunt. Moderate tricuspid regurgitation may also have masked the presence of the L‐R shunt. Although the Qp/Qs ratio suggested the presence of an L‐R shunt at the initial RHC examination, the inconsistency of the values in the oximetry assessment made it difficult to reach an accurate diagnosis. In fact, the inconsistency may be caused by both atrial and ventricular septal defects and tricuspid regurgitation. However, we should have tried to explore the intracardiac shunts by using multimodality imaging approaches. Previously, a similar case report explained that an unknown ASD was detected following the treatment of portal PH [ ]. The authors stated that hemodynamic changes (PVR↓, RA pressure↓, cardiac output↑, and pulmonary arterial wedge pressure [PAWP]↑) after PAH‐targeted therapy increased the L‐R shunt flow. In our case, PAP and PVR decreased, but RA pressure and RV end‐diastolic pressure slightly increased, and PAWP remained unchanged. Previously, a similar case report explained that an unknown ASD was detected following the treatment of portal PH [ ]. The authors stated that hemodynamic changes (PVR↓, RA pressure↓, cardiac output↑, and pulmonary arterial wedge pressure [PAWP]↑) after PAH‐targeted therapy increased the L‐R shunt flow. In our case, PAP and PVR decreased, but RA pressure and RV end‐diastolic pressure slightly increased, and PAWP remained unchanged. However, since the RV stroke volume/RV end‐diastolic pressure ratio has improved, it may theoretically reflect an improvement in RV compliance. We hypothesize that the improvement in RV compliance in this case has resulted in the emergence of the L‐R shunt. It was also noted that there may be several causes of PAH in a patient, and we should consider the possibility of unknown shunt disease in all PH cases during the PAH‐specific treatment. 5.3 Defect Closure in <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">PH</styled-content> Associated With <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">ASD</styled-content> and Clinical Course After Closure After catheter closure of ASD, further improvement of PH was observed in the patients who were treated with PAH‐specific medication [ , ]. Meta‐analyses also showed that both PH prevalence and mean PAP decrease after ASD closure [ ]. Closure with a fenestrated device may be safe and effective in PAH patients [ , ]. ASD closure was associated with improved long‐term survival even in ASD patients with PH (PVR < 5 WU) and even in patients over 40 years [ ]. According to the meta‐analysis, effective shunt closure by the treat‐and‐repair technique can improve hemodynamic and functional parameters with a low risk of MACEs even in ASD patients with severe PAH (PVR ≥ 5 WU) [ ]. Long‐term follow‐up after closure is mandatory in such severe PAH. It should be noted that the ESC guidelines indicated that patients with a persistent PVR ≥ 5 WU despite adequate medication are not recommended for defect closure. Fortunately, the clinical course in this case was favorable. Author Contributions Takaaki Fujii: data curation, investigation, visualization, writing – original draft.
